caption_en: 8. Room (k): the tunnel communicating between this room and the corridor (w) of the lower floor was closed in ancient times with a stone wall. The lower part of a bronze statue and fragments of ivory pertaining to furniture, 79 globes of amber, and a bronze wire with six globes of rock crystal in the shape of a pear and six spherical of carnelian were found.

9. Tablinum (n): the floor in wrought travertine flakes dates back to the first style. The long threshold, with the knock towards the atrium, is made of limestone slabs and preserves the recesses for the ups and downs of the four doors of the door.

10-11. Triclinium (s): the N wall, interrupted by a large quadrangular window, is the only one to retain traces of the IV style decoration with a uniformly black background. The plinth is divided into panels crossed by carpet edges and compartments that are now illegible. The middle area was divided into panels with vignettes, separated by compartments crossed by candelabra with squares. From Mau's brief description (Mau, in RM 1888, p. 185) we learn that the cartoons had griffins and panthers as their subjects and that in the center of this wall there was "some sacellum".

The plinth is divided into panels crossed by carpet edges and compartments that are now illegible. The middle area was divided into panels with vignettes, separated by compartments crossed by candelabra with squares. From Mau's brief description (Mau, in RM 1888, p. 185) we learn that the cartoons had griffins and panthers as their subjects and that in the center of this wall there was "some sacellum".

12. Triclinium (s), wall O: the central panel of the black plinth contains a large lozenge that perhaps served as a frame for a vignette; the middle area here has a bipartite structure with a central compartment crossed by a candelabra, between side panels with teardrop carpet edges.  77 N44983
13. Antechamber (v), on the lower floor, wall N: in corner W there remains a small fragment of the black plinth with a panel crossed by a square carpet border.
14. Antechamber (v), wall O: in the N corner next to the panel with a square carpet border is the compartment with purple bucranium.
15. Nymphaeum (x), on the lower floor: the flooring of this underground room but illuminated through the open window to the S, was made of rectangular slabs of tuff bordered by bands of marble.

16. Nymphaeum (x): the N wall was built in such a way as to appear as a cave from which the water flows and falls into the basin in front. In fact, the vault and the interior of the niche are covered with fragments of Sarno limestone while the external wall of the basin was painted with Nilotic and marine scenes. On the whole, the fertilizing floods of the Nile were evoked, from the waterfalls between the rocks of Upper Egypt to the stagnant calm of the Delta. The remaining walls were covered with a low tuff plinth on which white marble slabs rested; the S wall near the window was plastered white.

17. Nymphaeum (x): the niche with the vault, the walls and the side slides covered with Sarno limestone; the ladder on which the water flowed was covered with marble, while the vertical section of the wall, with the outlet of the pipe, was painted in reddish stucco with irregular yellow and red stripes that are found on the back wall of the pool at the end of the ladder, indicating the path of the water. The jambs and probably the arch ring were covered with mosaic.

18. Nymphaeum (x): detail of jamb O of the niche, covered in mosaic with blue and yellow glass paste tiles, with shells of cardium edule along the outer edge. The scarce preserved elements do not allow the decorative motif to be recognized, probably large carpet edges or geometric elements.

19. Nymphaeum (x), section W of the external wall of the basin with a niche at the flat bottom in which a uraeus is painted; On the stretch of the right forepart you can see the remains of a Nilotic landscape with aquatic plants and a reed fence in the background.

20. Nymphaeum (x): the extreme W section of the basin preserves illegible traces of a Nilotic landscape. Between the podium and the wall you can see one of the white marble slabs on the low tuff plinth that made up the wall covering of the room.
21. Nymphaeum (x): the left cheek of niche O has a tuft of marsh plants with long lanceolate leaves in the lower part above which the watercourse can be seen.
22. Nymphaeum (x): the right cheek of the O niche and the E section of the external wall with traces of a Nilotic landscape.

23. Nymphaeum (x): traces of the painted decoration are still found in niche E of the basin where a faux marble slab can be recognized next to a narrow square with margins engraved in the fresh plaster.

24. Nymphaeum (x), W wall: in the N corner, above the basin there remains a band of stucco with incrustations of marble fragments; at the bottom is recognizable the plaster prepared for the adhesion of marble slabs.
25. Nymphaeum (x): detail of the attachment of the vault on the niche, where the pseudo-cave covering obtained with the limestone of the Sarno has been better preserved.
26. Procoeton (y): the entrance from the annular corridor (w) to this room is through a narrow arched passage plastered in white; the masonry steps are covered with cocciopesto. 77 N45003 V.S.

1. The N façade of the house, completely rebuilt around the middle of the first century B.C. in opus reticulata with recurrences of bricks and jambs in opus vittata mista, with the kitchen window (a) and the latrine window (b). The presence of the drawing of a lying anchor and other geometric motifs, obtained with the use of tufelli of different colors, has been repeatedly taken in support of the hypothesis that the reticulated work could also not be plastered, but Mau (Mau, in BdI, 1884, p. 215) already observed that on this same wall there were traces, albeit minimal,  of plaster.
2. Under the open window of the latrine (b), on the external façade, there is a comic terracotta mask.

3. Vestibule (1) of the entrance at number 29: the mosaic flooring of the room was made at the same time as that of the atrium towards which it rises, in the Claudian age. On a carpet of black tesserae arranged in a straight warp dotted with large white tesserae, and with a wide, double white border, rows of rhomboidal tiles of red and triangular and square marbles of green and yellow marbles are aligned.  78 N62702
4. Atrium (x), section N: white mosaic floor, with tesserae arranged in an oblique warp and regular rows of large black tesserae.

5. Room ({): the floor in beaten limestone flakes bedded in white mortar dates back to the period of the second style, and was preserved even when the wall structures of the room were subsequently modified.

6. Vestibule (A) of the entrance at number 30: the fragment of the cocciopesto pavement with meanders alternating with concentric squares is one of the scarce still preserved testimonies of the dating to the Samnite era of the primitive layout of this house. The detail of the rendering of the squares in rows of black tesserae is one of the elements that supports this dating. Completely lost is the scale motif still seen by Pernice in the center of the room.   77 N44878

7. Atrium (4): the floor, traced back by Mau to the first style, by Lehmann-Hartleben in the middle of the first century A.D. and which comes from Pernice (Partridge, p. 73) placed in the first century B.C., consists of a grayish mortar in which flakes of different sizes are bedded, of gray and gray-blue limestone with, in smaller quantities, yellow,  white and red.

8. Cubicle (d): the decoration of the fourth style with the middle area with a bipartite structure with red panels separated by a compartment with a white background crossed by a thin candelabrum, was never completed with the plinth.

9. The room (f) must initially have had a different function from the one later reserved for it as a storage room with shelves on the walls. In fact, it had a white mosaic floor with a black border and the upper part of the walls had been painted but had stopped leaving the rest to rough plaster.

10. Wing (g): the threshold "a white mosaic with black and red ornaments" seen by Mau (Mau, in BdI, 1885, p. 86) no longer existed in the '30s (Pernice, p. 74), while the travertine pavement bedridden in grayish mortar is still preserved.

11. Ala(g), N wall: the middle area has a simple decoration of yellow panels with carpet borders and squares, separated by an architectural glimpse with a white background, while the plinth was covered with rough plaster, prepared for the application of marble slabs according to a program of embellishment of the house underway in the last months of the city's life,  which had also led to the covering with marble of the staircase of (E), the plinth of the other wing (H) and the floors of (P), (Q), (S) in which, however, only the imprints and some minimal fragments of the marbles used were found.
12. Wing (g), S wall, with the door towards (o) closed before the plaster for the IV style decoration was applied, identical to that of the opposite wall.

13. Ala(g), wall O: the greater length of the wall allows the decorative scheme to be expanded into a symmetrical structure with a large central panel separated from the side panels by architectural views with a white background closed at the bottom by partitions.

14. Wing (h), N wall: the decoration of the fourth style reproduced the scheme of that of the wing (g) with yellow panels separated by rather simple architectural views. The plinth had been left rough to apply marble slabs.

15. Wing (h): the E wall is interrupted by the access door to the staircase (t) through which the floor below was reached, but to access it it was necessary to overcome a difference in height of about 80 cm filled by the podium of a ladder leaning against the S-E corner of the room.
16. Wing (h), S wall: in the yellow panels of the middle area there were small pictures, of which there is no news, detached from the first excavators.

17. Cubicle (i), wall E: the black plinth retains no trace of the decorative motifs; the middle area has a narrow red panel in the center separated from the yellow side panels by compartments with a white background. The small paintings (height 11.5 cm, width 37 cm) with a blue background which, according to Mau's description (Mau, in Bd, 1885, p. 94), were on this wall are totally illegible. In the one on the left there was a female mask with ònkos facing right, and that of a bald old man with a thick white beard, facing in the same direction. In the small picture on the right there were two female masks, one almost in front of the other time on the left, and another of an old man.

18. Cubicle (i), S wall: the central panel of the middle area, with a red background, showed a small picture (height 11.2 cm, width 34) illegible, like the small medallions (diameter 14 cm) present in the yellow panels.
19. Room (k): the cocciopesto floor with hexagonal, square and triangular limestone tiles.

20. Room (k), wall N: Mau (Mau, in Bd, 1885, p. 91) already emphasized the monotony of the decoration of the rooms of this house, even if carried out "not without diligence, nor without good taste". On the black plinth, a compartment with a white background separates the yellow panels, on one of which a carpet is stretched, with rectangular squares whose subject is illegible.

21. Room (k), wall E: an architectural view that develops behind a low architraved aedicule, separates two panels with yellow stretched carpets that exhibit two small paintings with masks in the center. In the left one (height 13 cm, width 33.5) the masks of Perseus and Andromeda with the bleeding sea monster were recognized; in the right one (height 13 cm, width 33.5) the masks of a Silenus crowned with leaves and a bearded man with a cap on his head.

22. Room (k), wall S: in the panels of the black plinth there are barely rectangular squares. In the middle area, the yellow stretched carpet panel is separated from the red panel with semicircular and squared carpet edges by a narrow white compartment.

23. Cubicle (I), wall N: it is evident in this case that the possibility of obtaining decorative effects with the use of tufelli of different colors, in the construction of the reticulated work, did not prevent it from being covered with plaster.
24. Cubicle (1), wall E: the completely discoloured plinth was probably black, the central panel of the middle area, with a medallion (diameter 18 cm), is yellow, and the side panels are red.

25. Cubicle (1), W wall, with large window towards the atrium. The black plinth is divided into panels by narrow squares outlined in red; in the middle area the usual tripartition of yellow panels in the center and red on the sides.

26. Cubicle (1), S wall: the panels of the black plinth were divided by red squares; in the middle area, the panel on the left with a square carpet border contains a square (height 18 cm, width 33 cm) and the right panel with a yellow stretched carpet contains a medallion (diameter 21.5 cm).

27. Cubicle (n): N wall with the open window towards the street. The plinth and the middle area have the same structure, with a central compartment and side panels. In the red ones with carpet edges in the middle area there were small rectangular squares characteristic of the decoration of this house.

28. Cubicle (n), wall E in which it is evident that the reticulated opus wall was erected on a previous uncertain opus wall. Here too the square (height 10 cm, width 23 cm) of the red middle area is totally illegible.

29. Cubicle (n): the S wall with the door to the atrium had been rebuilt in brick work and with the jamb in opus vittata; the plinth is red, the panel of the middle area, with the square (height 10 cm, width 26 cm), is yellow.

30. Cubicle (n), wall O: the small residue of plaster in the upper area allows us to recognize that it was on a white background; the panels of the middle area are instead with a red background and separated by a narrow black compartment.

31. Cubicle (11) on the 1st floor below: N wall with the kidneys of the vault below the terrace that was to cover all the rooms on the lower floor. The fall of the pictorial layers highlighted the underlying rough plaster speckled for the adhesion of the surface layers.

32. Cubicle (11), wall E: the position of this room, at the end of the corridor (15), the only source of lighting, required the walls to be painted white. In fact, only the plinth is black, while the middle area stretches out into large panels squared by stretched garlands and separated by a narrow compartment also with a white background, like the bezel. '78 N62721
33. Cubicle (11), wall E: detail of the lunette with a lower frame of circumscribed trefoils closed at the bottom by lying S.

34. Cubicle (12) on the 1st floor below, wall O: the location of this room, similar to that of the cubicle (11), also led to the choice of white as the background color of the walls, which had simple and thin red squares to outline the panels and distinguish the middle area from the plinth and the lunette.

35. Triclinium (16), N wall in opus incerta in which limestone blocks obtained from the bare of the walls are inserted. The middle area had a paratactic articulation with red panels squared by edges of carpet in circles, separated by narrow white compartments. The right panel is heavily blackened. On the floor of this room, in cocciopesto with scattered limestone tiles, Mau (Mau, in BdI, 1885, p. 92) read a few letters of an already mutilated inscription, completely lost in the '30s (Pernice, p. 73).

36. Triclinium (16), O wall: the plinth had an elegant imitation of marble inlays including imitation serpentine medallions. In the middle area, the alternation of red panels and white compartments was repeated.

37. Triclinium (17), on the 1st floor below, wall N: with the exception of the plinth painted in black, the walls and vault of this room were uniformly yellow with a network of swastika meanders and red squares that unfolded continuously over all surfaces.  77 N45004

38. Triclinium (17): Niccolini's panel reproduces a detail of the continuous decoration of this room with the faithful restitution of the colors and the detail of the four-petal rosette in the squares.

39-40. Triclinium (17) of the 1st floor below, wall E: the high plinth with a black background has a sequence of panels and compartments that is not matched in the middle area with a continuous structure. In the panels, there are triangle carpet edges, a medallion and a rectangle. The stucco cornice that separates the middle area from the vault, in which the same mesh decoration of meanders and squares is taken up, is made of trefoils circumscribed by volutes.

39-40. Triclinium (17) of the 1st floor below, wall E: the high plinth with a black background has a sequence of panels and compartments that is not matched in the middle area with a continuous structure. In the panels, there are triangle carpet edges, a medallion and a rectangle. The stucco cornice that separates the middle area from the vault, in which the same mesh decoration of meanders and squares is taken up, is made of trefoils circumscribed by volutes.

41. Triclinium (17), wall O: black plinth with panels and compartments. In the left panel you can see the edge of a triangle carpet, in the right one the medallion in which it seems to recognize the traces of a bust (?).
1. The section of the façade to the E of the door, in uncertain work, preserves remains of the decoration in the first style with orthostats and stucco ashlars in relief.  '78 N44080

2. Vestibule (b): the cocciopesto floor has a motif of scales and the threshold towards the atrium swastika meanders alternating with concentric squares, partly damaged by the insertion of the threshold in six pieces of white marble veined with gray, equipped at the ends with recesses for the hinges but without those for the bolts as the door leaves were stopped together by the lock.
3. Vestibule (b): on wall E remains the primitive decoration in the first style with ashlars engraved in the plaster.

4. Atrium (c): the black mosaic floor with regular rows of white tesserae and crosses had two white bands as its edge and around the impluvium a guilloche defined by Mau (Mau, in RM, 1886, p. 149) as "white Greek". It was built after the insertion of the threshold towards the vestibule on which it rests.
5. Cubicle (e): the cocciopesto floor dates back to the first style with regular rows of white tesserae that extend almost to the limits of the field.  77 N44912
6. Cubicle (f): absolutely similar to the previous one is the cocciopesto floor with dotted white tiles.

7. Cubicle (f), wall N: the red plinth had plants in the panels separated from the central compartment; the white middle area, with a bipartite structure, exhibited a candelabrum in the central compartment of which barely a trace remains.

8. Cubicle (f): wall E, the one with the largest painted surface in the room, had a plinth divided into panels and compartments placed below those of the middle area which in the central panel had a painting (height 37 cm, width 39 cm) completely illegible.
9. Cubicle (f), wall E, section S: detail of the red plinth with flowering bush.

10. Cubicle (f), wall S: although the conservation conditions are better than on the opposite one, no other decorative details can be identified other than the bushes in the plinth, and the candelabra in the central compartment, even if in the side panels it seems to identify two vignettes in the center of each of the panels of the middle area.

11. Cubicle (f), wall W with the door to the atrium (c) in which there is the mouth of the cistern located N of the impluvium. In the red hoof you can recognize the bushes; the panels of the middle area with edges of a triangle carpet, preserved only horizontally, showed completely illegible vignettes in the center. In the S section, on direct view, the traces of the preparatory engravings of an architectural landscape can be identified.

12. Cubicle (g): in the cocciopesto floor with white tesserae, one can recognize the desire to differentiate the field with scattered tesserae and flakes, relegated only to the limits near the wall, by the carpet with a net of lozenges, bordered by the edge of two rows of tiles placed side by side, which give it particular elegance. The travertine threshold with the hinges of the double-leaf door that opened towards the inside of the room, supported, like those of all the other rooms around the atrium, another door to the same.

13. Cubicle (g), wall N: the red plinth has a simple geometric partition in the panels; in the middle area, the red central panel is separated from the yellow side panels by narrow white compartments; the upper area, completely

14. Cubicle (g), wall E with the large gap caused by previous excavators, perhaps the cunicularii returned after the eruption; it has the same decorative scheme as the adjoining N wall. The division of the plinth into overlapping rectangles is more evident here.
15. Cubicle (g), S wall: the gaps in the painted plaster have highlighted the preparation layers.

16. Cubicle (g), wall O with the door and the threshold in which the pairs of circular recesses to house the hinges and the engraving for the wooden cladding of the jambs in blocks of limestone from Sarno, dating back to the first planting of the house, can be distinguished.

17. Wing (h): the floor in well-bedded travertine flakes was separated from that of the atrium by the mosaic threshold, 0.58 m wide, in which the white and black tiles alternate in a checkerboard pattern, and which is bordered around by a narrow band of two rows of brick tiles, which gives a singular and lively note of polychromy to the severe floor dating back to the end of the second century BC,  among the IIstyle.
18. Cubicle (k): cocciopesto floor with a network of swastika meanders, alternating with squares with a white central cross.

19. Cubicle (k): the gaps in the rough plaster highlight a restoration with ceramic fragments and tuff blocks in the N wall in opus incerta. At the time of the excavation, in this room in which the mouth of a cistern placed near the door had been closed, only a fragment of a black plinth was preserved on the same wall E.

20. Tablinum (m): white mosaic with tesserae arranged in a straight warp; The threshold towards the atrium consists of a swastika meander motif with squares with a central cross outlined in black in a very large design. In the center there was the emblem with a checkerboard medallion and four geese in the resulting corners, dating back, like the rest of the flooring, to the second style.

21. Tablinum (m): the emblem (105 x 105 cm) is now in the Museum of Naples (inv. 114280). The central medallion consists of a checkerboard combination of black and white triangles and squares inserted successively and with larger tesserae in a border formed by a polychrome two-stranded braid, probably on the occasion of a restoration also carried out on some parts of the birds. The guilloche is given prominence thanks to the use, along the margin, of gray and beige tesserae; The center is alternately gray and red with a white center tile. The brown outer circular frame merges with the square frame in which the medallion is inserted. In the resulting triangular sectors are depicted four Egyptian geese, seen from the front and with open wings in the characteristic pose INS. 2, 34-35

22. Triclinium (n): the floor, now very little preserved, was a white mosaic with tesserae arranged in an oblique warp and without any border, attributable to the II style, but the very famous emblem with doves on a gilded bronze basin in its center can still be dated to the first style.

23. Triclinium (n): the emblem, derived from a model by Sosos, is now in the Museum of Naples (inv. 114281); it is in almost excellent condition, with small gaps in the black bottom and inside the basin, at the second pigeon from the right. On a marble surface rests a basin with lion's paws and surmounting handles, near which are two specimens of columba livia, while three others rest on the edge and a fifth arrives in flight from the left. The birds are well characterized in their white, gray and light brown plumage; the reflections of the water are rendered with yellow and gray tesserae, but the reflection of the pigeon bending down to drink is missing compared to the original by Sosos of Pergamon, admired by Pliny (Nat. hist., XXXVI, 184). 24. Triclinium (0): in the center of the white mosaic floor with a black border, on which the staircase to the upper floor was later placed, there was the emblem with lion and panther now in the Museum of Naples (inv. 114282). The depiction is rather ruined by long oblique lesions but the scene is well recognizable even if not complete in all details. A lion, seen from the front, so that the body is for the most part covered by the large head, with the exception of the right hind paw firmly resting on the ground, has landed and holds still a spotted panther, wounded in the abdomen from which the blood flows, which turns its gaze upwards. The assault took place in a rocky landscape with small and sparse tufts of grass, near a stream from which the panther had perhaps gone to drink. In the background on the right, a tree gives substance to the landscape that is lost in the background due to the fading of yellowish and beige tones with the white of the sky. Remarkable, although the figure of the pan-tera is not complete (the hind legs in fact go beyond the limits of the frame), the rendering of naturalistic details and animal expressions. The feline's spots are rendered in blue but overall they are fully realistic, as is the desperate but proud expression of his gaze. The derivation of the subject (although the composition is different due to the presence of two animals in this one) from the same model to which INS was based is evident. 2, 34-35

25. Room (v), wall N: the room, located at street level and therefore at a lower level than the rest of the house and the adjoining room (d), was once open to the outside. The masonry in blocks of limestone from Sarno and the decoration in the first style, of which part of the white and red stucco of the upper area remains, attest to the antiquity of its construction.

26. Room (a) on the 1st floor below derives, with the adjoining (B), from the subdivision of a single large room also extending towards the S to include part of the corridor (£), which had a unitary decoration, with a high yellow plinth, and a black middle area separated by a red band, to which the dividing partitions were superimposed. 27. Room (a): the wall E, which is a thin dividing partition, was covered with simple white plaster in which you can see the trace of the floor of the upper mezzanine accessible only by portable ladders, which were approached to the entrance on the S front. In the background are the remains of the original decoration preserved on the E wall of the room (B).

28-29. Room (0): in the N section of the W wall remains the recess of the bed arranged on the mezzanine obtained above the door, near which traces of the II style decoration can be distinguished with the high yellow plinth, surmounted by two bands, one red and one black; on the floor above the black plinth and the white middle area could be distinguished, evidently derived from what in the primitive organization of the environment had been the upper area.

28-29. Room (0): in the N section of the W wall remains the recess of the bed arranged on the mezzanine obtained above the door, near which traces of the II style decoration can be distinguished with the high yellow plinth, surmounted by two bands, one red and one black; on the floor above the black plinth and the white middle area could be distinguished, evidently derived from what in the primitive organization of the environment had been the upper area.
30. Room (p), N wall: the yellow plinth reached a height of 1.52 m up to the red band that distinguished it from the middle area in which sturdy support beams were inserted for the mezzanine floor.
31. Room (B): wall E is perhaps the best preserved of this room; above the black middle area, the upper white area can still be partially distinguished.

32. Room (B): wall O consists of the added partition covered with signino plaster. On the west wall of the nearby room (£) is the ring of tuff ashlars of the vault that had once covered what had originally been a single large room, and which in the internal division of the space had been replaced by flat ceilings.

33. The cubicle (Y) on the 1st floor below, which retains a decoration considered contemporary with that of the candelabra of the nearby triclinium ($), but which Mau himself (Mau, in RM, 1886, p. 154) has judged to be similar to the II style, in the last years of its life was destined for another use, as would seem to be proven by the series of holes,  present in the N wall, to house large beams. Their shallow depth, however, and the arrangement, did not facilitate the recognition of the use of the room itself. Above a high red plinth with a yellow end frame, whose mouldings are rendered in light brown, the green middle area unfolds, closed at the top by a white band with a fake red frame that marks the beginning of the upper red area.  '77 N45019

34. Cubicle (Y): detail of the N-E corner with the red plinth, the high moulded frame rendered in yellow, and the green middle area framed by white borders, in which traces of engravings can be seen, including that of a circle traced with a compass.

35-36. The room (è), which at the time of the documentation (1977) was partly reburied, had a concrete floor decorated with white tiles to indicate the arrangement of the triclinium beds; it is located at the end of the corridor (£), and is oriented with the entrance to the W so that the N wall is one of the long sides. The III style decoration with candelabra had a red plinth; the black middle area articulated in panels, but devoid of any ornamental element, ended at the top with a frieze with a black background between red, white and yellow bands; the upper area was white.

The room (è), which at the time of the documentation (1977) was partly reburied, had a concrete floor decorated with white tiles to indicate the arrangement of the triclinium beds; it is located at the end of the corridor (£), and is oriented with the entrance to the W so that the N wall is one of the long sides. The III style decoration with candelabra had a red plinth; the black middle area articulated in panels, but devoid of any ornamental element, ended at the top with a frieze with a black background between red, white and yellow bands; the upper area was white.

37. Room (is): on the E wall you can follow the lowered arch course of the completely collapsed vault; other holes for shelving in the middle area are also evident which, together with a pillar leaning against the S wall, attest to a use of the room no longer for living but for utilitarianism.

38. Room (is), wall O: the decoration of this room was defined by Mau (Mau, in RM 1886, p. 154) as "simple, without diligence in execution and without exquisiteness of taste either in design or in colors"; the detachment between the black middle area and the white upper area is established by a black frieze bordered by narrow red bands.

39. Corridor (€), S wall: on the structure in opus incerta of Sarno limestone, a decoration of the III style was laid that imitated the I in the distribution, above the plinth, of orthostats and rows of ashlars arranged in red and black outlined in red and black.
40. Corridor (€), wall O with the door to the ramp (u) of descent to this floor below. Above the door there is a closed rectangular window, framed in the ashlar and limestone ferrule.

41. Triclinium (0): the large room that constituted the centre of the residential sector on the lower floor, retained, above the black plinth, purple panels with a blue border similar to the II style, although Mau (Mau, in RM, 1886, p. 155) defined the decoration as "candelabra" with a purple background. It was covered by a barrel vault that also included two narrow side rooms, the corridor (n) and the tunnel (1), perhaps a wardrobe that ended with a small window open towards (£); the floor was in cocciopesto with polychrome crustae and a well-executed meander threshold of white tesserae separated the antechamber from the room.

7. Triclinium (6), wall N: central painting (92 x 82 cm) with Apollo and Daphne, also reproduced by G. Abbate (ADS 830; see Disegnatori, p. 260, fig. 39). The god, with a laurel wreath, is seated on a rock, covered by a red mantle and aZZurro, holds the nine-stringed zither with his left, has his right arm (badly executed) folded over his head and looks towards Daphne who, standing, leans with her right hand on the same group of rocks; she is covered by a yellow and violet mantle that falls behind her shoulders. She has a necklace, bracelets and earrings, a laurel wreath on her head and twigs of the same plant sprouting on her shoulders. It is the adaptation of a scheme usually used for other characters, given the serene attitude of the two protagonists; according to the most widespread myth, in fact, the young woman, trying to escape the god, found refuge with mother Earth who transformed her into the tree later favored by Apollo. The figures derive from statuary types such as that of Leochares' Apollo and Aphrodite standing.

In the workshop with entrance at no. 3 of Via dell'Abbondanza, from which it was possible to enter the atrium (2) of House VIII 4, 4, there was (according to Fiorelli's information, in GdS, 1861, p. 12) this depiction of Mercury with the bag, the caduceus and the ram, now in the Museo Naz. of Naples (inv. 9450; cf. the reproduction in Disegnatori, p. 426, fig. 26; Fiorelli, cit., tav. III, 3). The wall decoration of the workshop, with a green background, also included (Fiorelli, cit.) a figure of Fortuna with the rudder and the cornucopia, a deity that is well suited to the function of the environment. The rooms located along the perimeter of the insula (such as this workshop and the vestibule of the house, cf. figs. 4-11) were excavated a few years before the rest of the insula (cf. PAH, II, pp. 623 ff.) and to this circumstance we owe the fact that the figure of Mercury was detached (in 1855: cf. Fiorelli, cit.), while the rest of the decoration of the house was left în situ. This is an innovative choice made by Fiorelli certainly with the intention of not dividing the decoration, privileging, as had been done so far, the figurative part over the ornamental one, a choice that has, however, in fact condemned what was left în situ to abandonment: in the Introduction to the first issue of the Giornale degli Scavi (Fiorelli, in GdS, 1861, p. 1),  he writes: 'Thus stripped of their vaguest ornament (the paintings), many of those buildings once admirable for their prodigious preservation, now present the gloomy appearance of crumbling ruins, which would not be long in disappearing, if they were not rushed to with prompt and effective restorations'. These operations — which resulted in a sufficient preservation of the wall structures and the surface of the plaster — were not sufficient to protect the pictorial film, and the painted decoration was entirely lost.
